name: Slap bracelet
blurb: A flat steel band in a fabric cover that curled around your wrist when slapped, a 1990 fad
title: Slap Bracelets: The 1990 Craze and Why Schools Banned Them
description: Slap bracelets are steel bands in fabric covers that curl round the wrist when slapped. Sold as Slap Wraps, they were a 1990 craze until school bans.
answer: A slap bracelet is a straight strip of springy steel inside a fabric or plastic cover: hold it flat, slap it against your wrist and it instantly curls into a bracelet. Invented by Wisconsin teacher Stuart Anders and sold as Slap Wraps from 1990 for about $2.50, it became a huge school craze that year. Cheap knockoffs that cut children's wrists led to school bans and a recall, and the fad faded by the end of 1990, though slap bracelets are still made today.

body: Inside the cover are thin layers of stainless steel shaped like a tape measure. The band has two stable states: straight, or rolled up. Flatten it and it stays flat; give it a smack across the wrist and it snaps into a coil. The original Slap Wraps were about 23 cm long, 2.5 cm wide and made from steel 0.15 mm thick, covered in brightly patterned fabric.
Anders based the idea on a self-retracting tape measure. Big toy companies turned it down, and it was Main Street Toy Company of Simsbury, Connecticut, that brought it out.

rows: Stuart Anders comes up with the bracelet; the prototype sits unused for years
Slap Wraps draw attention at the American International Toy Fair in New York
Shipments finally reach stores after production delays
About 1 million Slap Wraps sell at $2.50 in three months; an estimated 10–15 million knockoffs follow, some for 70 cents
Injury reports lead schools in New York and Pennsylvania to ban them; Connecticut recalls imported versions

body: The trouble came mostly from cheap copies made with thinner steel. When the cover wore through, the sharp metal edge could cut skin, and a four-year-old in Wallingford, Connecticut, cut her finger on one. Connecticut's consumer protection department recalled the foreign-made versions, and the US Consumer Product Safety Commission told parents to check bracelets for frayed edges.
Some schools banned them outright after a child was cut; others banned them for being distracting, since slapping them on and off in class made noise. A few simply had teachers check for worn edges.

Yes. The original Slap Wraps did not last, and the company behind them nearly went under, but other manufacturers have kept making slap bracelets, including licensed character designs sold through big retailers. Safety problems have not entirely gone away: some products were recalled again in 2017 and 2018 because the metal could pierce the cover and cut young children.
